title: Product of the Last K Numbers

problem.description:
Design an algorithm that accepts a stream of integers and retrieves the product of the last k integers of the stream.

Implement the ProductOfNumbers class:

- ProductOfNumbers() Initializes the object with an empty stream.

- void add(int num) Appends the integer num to the stream.

- int getProduct(int k) Returns the product of the last k numbers in the current list. You can assume that always the current list has at least k numbers.

The test cases are generated so that, at any time, the product of any contiguous sequence of numbers will fit into a single 32-bit integer without overflowing.

Example:

Input
["ProductOfNumbers","add","add","add","add","add","getProduct","getProduct","getProduct","add","getProduct"]
[[],[3],[0],[2],[5],[4],[2],[3],[4],[8],[2]]

Output
[null,null,null,null,null,null,20,40,0,null,32]

Explanation
ProductOfNumbers productOfNumbers = new ProductOfNumbers();
productOfNumbers.add(3);        // [3]
productOfNumbers.add(0);        // [3,0]
productOfNumbers.add(2);        // [3,0,2]
productOfNumbers.add(5);        // [3,0,2,5]
productOfNumbers.add(4);        // [3,0,2,5,4]
productOfNumbers.getProduct(2); // return 20. The product of the last 2 numbers is 5 * 4 = 20
productOfNumbers.getProduct(3); // return 40. The product of the last 3 numbers is 2 * 5 * 4 = 40
productOfNumbers.getProduct(4); // return 0. The product of the last 4 numbers is 0 * 2 * 5 * 4 = 0
productOfNumbers.add(8);        // [3,0,2,5,4,8]
productOfNumbers.getProduct(2); // return 32. The product of the last 2 numbers is 4 * 8 = 32

Constraints:

- 0 <= num <= 100

- 1 <= k <= 4 * 10^4

- At most 4 * 10^4 calls will be made to add and getProduct.

- The product of the stream at any point in time will fit in a 32-bit integer.

Follow-up: Can you implement both GetProduct and Add to work in O(1) time complexity instead of O(k) time complexity?

hints: Numbers keep arriving one at a time, and at any moment you may be asked to multiply together the most recent `k` of them. You want both adding a number and answering a query to be cheap.

In the example, any query whose window reaches back over the `0` returns 0, no matter what else is in it. Queries that stay entirely after the `0` behave as if the earlier part of the stream never existed.

There can be up to `4 * 10^4` calls, and each `k` can be up to `4 * 10^4`. Multiplying the last `k` numbers on every query costs `O(k)`, which is about `1.6 * 10^9` operations in the worst case and too slow. You want `O(1)` per operation.

This is a running prefix product, the multiplicative cousin of prefix sums. A product over a range can be recovered by dividing one prefix product by an earlier one, just as a range sum is a difference of prefix sums.

Division breaks when a zero is involved, so whenever a `0` arrives, throw away all history and start fresh. If a query's `k` reaches back to or past that reset point, the window must contain the zero, so the answer is 0.

Keep a list of prefix products that starts with a sentinel `1`. Each entry is the product of all numbers added since the most recent zero, up to that position. The list's length minus one tells you how many nonzero numbers have arrived since the last zero.

On `add(num)` with `num` equal to 0: reset the list to just `[1]`.
On `add(num)` with any other value: append `last entry * num` to the list.
On `getProduct(k)`: let `n` be the list length.
If `k >= n`, return 0, because the window includes a zero.
Otherwise, return `list[n-1] / list[n-1-k]`.

The trickiest part is the boundary check: use `k >= n`, not `k > n`, because the sentinel occupies one slot. Also handle a zero as the very first number, and several zeros in a row; resetting handles both. The guarantee that products fit in 32 bits keeps the stored prefixes safe from overflow. Each `add` and `getProduct` runs in `O(1)` time (amortized for list appends), and space is `O(n)` for the stored prefixes.

normal.note: Simple prefix products with no zeros.
Interleaved adds and queries with ones.
Multiple zeros, only last segment matters.
Query whole stream after extra add.

edge.note: Single element: one add and k=1.
Single zero: product of only element is 0.
Zero last: every query includes it.
All zeros: every product is 0; large case would be 4*10^4 such calls.

approach.oneLiner: Support appending non-negative integers to a list and answering, at any time, the product of the last `k` appended integers.
signals: "product of the last k numbers" means a contiguous suffix → this is a range query, so precompute prefix products and divide, the same way prefix sums answer range sums.
`0 <= num <= 100`, so zeros can appear → division by a prefix that contains 0 breaks. Any window that covers a 0 has product 0, so only the stretch after the most recent zero matters.
Follow-up asks for O(1) `add` and `getProduct` → each query must be answered from stored state, not by rescanning `k` elements.

"product of any contiguous sequence ... fits in a 32-bit integer" → a prefix product that starts right after the last zero is itself a contiguous product, so it never overflows. That only holds if the prefix restarts at zeros.
approach.constraints: Up to 4·10^4 calls with `k` up to 4·10^4. Rescanning `k` numbers per query is about 4·10^4 × 4·10^4 = 1.6·10^9 multiplications in the worst case, which is too slow. O(1) per call means about 4·10^4 total operations, so the target is O(1) amortised per operation.

thinking.q: What is the most direct way to answer `getProduct(k)`?
thinking.a: Keep every number in a list and multiply the last `k` of them. That is correct but costs O(k) per query, up to 1.6·10^9 work overall.

thinking.q: Suffix product queries look like suffix sum queries. What is the standard trick there?
thinking.a: Store prefix sums and subtract. For products, store `prefix[i]` = product of the first `i` numbers, then answer with `prefix[n] / prefix[n-k]`.

thinking.q: Why does plain prefix-product division fail on the example `[3,0,2,5,4]`?
thinking.a: After the 0, every prefix is 0. `getProduct(2)` would compute `0 / 0` instead of 20. Dividing out a zero is impossible.

thinking.q: What does a zero really tell us about future queries?
thinking.a: Any window that reaches back to or past that zero has product 0. Windows that stay strictly after it never involve anything before it. So everything before the latest zero can be forgotten.

thinking.q: So how should the prefix array behave when `num == 0` arrives?
thinking.a: Reset it to `[1]`, so prefixes start fresh after the zero. Its length minus one is now the count of numbers since the last zero. If `k` is at least the prefix length, the window includes that zero and the answer is 0. Otherwise the answer is `prefix[last] / prefix[last-k]`.

approaches.name: Store list, multiply last k
approaches.aha: The problem literally says "product of the last k numbers", so the first instinct is to keep the stream and loop over its tail.
approaches.idea: Append each `num` to a list. For `getProduct(k)`, multiply the last `k` elements. It is trivially correct because it computes exactly the definition. You can stop early when you hit a 0.
steps: Loop over the last `k` entries, multiplying into `p`. Return 0 immediately if an entry is 0.
approaches.complexity: The loop over `k` elements in each query dominates. With 4·10^4 queries of `k` = 4·10^4 that is about 1.6·10^9 steps. The list holds every added number.
approaches.tradeoff: Each query redoes multiplications that earlier queries already did. Worst case 1.6·10^9 operations is too slow and fails the O(1) follow-up.

approaches.name: List plus last-zero index
approaches.aha: The brute force walks all the way to a zero just to return 0. If we remember where the most recent zero is, we can answer those queries instantly.
approaches.idea: Alongside the list, store `lastZero`, the index of the most recent 0 (or -1 if none). If `k > n - 1 - lastZero`, the window includes that zero, so return 0 at once. Otherwise multiply the last `k` numbers, which are all non-zero. This is correct because any window containing a 0 has product 0. It is still O(k) when the window contains no zero.
steps: `add(num)`: append it. If `num == 0`, set `lastZero` to its index.
Otherwise multiply `nums[n-k .. n-1]` and return the product.
approaches.time: O(1) add, O(k) getProduct worst case
approaches.complexity: Queries whose window covers a zero become O(1). Zero-free windows still cost O(k), so the worst case is unchanged. The list stores the whole stream.
approaches.tradeoff: A long stretch of 1s with no zeros still forces O(k) multiplication per query, about 1.6·10^9 in the worst case. We still recompute overlapping suffix products every time.

approaches.name: Prefix products reset on zero
approaches.aha: The Better approach already showed that nothing before the last zero matters. The products after it overlap from query to query, so precompute them as prefix products and divide.
approaches.idea: Maintain `prefix`, starting as `[1]`, where `prefix[i]` is the product of the first `i` numbers since the most recent zero. On `add(0)`, reset `prefix` to `[1]`. Otherwise append `prefix[last] * num`. For `getProduct(k)`: if `k >= prefix.length`, the window reaches the zero (or the very start before any zero, which k never exceeds), so return 0. Otherwise return `prefix[last] / prefix[last - k]`. The division is exact and never divides by 0, because all stored factors are non-zero. Each prefix is a contiguous product, so it fits in 32 bits.
steps: If `k >= m`, return 0, because the window includes the last zero.
approaches.time: O(1) per add and getProduct (amortised for append)
approaches.complexity: Each operation does one append or one array lookup plus one division, so the work is constant. The `prefix` array holds at most one entry per number added since the last zero.
approaches.tradeoff: Every query needs at least constant time, so this cannot be beaten asymptotically. The cost is O(n) memory, which the Better approach also needed. The method also relies on exact integer division, which only works because the zeros were removed.

mistakes: Not handling zeros and dividing `prefix[n]/prefix[n-k]` when the prefix includes a 0. This gives division by zero or a wrong 0 for windows that lie after the zero, such as `getProduct(2) = 20` in the example.
Off-by-one in the zero check. With `prefix = [1, a, b]`, `k = 2` is valid (`b*a/1`), while `k = 3` reaches the zero and must return 0. The condition is `k >= prefix.length`, not `k > prefix.length`.

Keeping one global prefix product across zeros by skipping zeros instead of resetting. Windows that span a zero then return a non-zero value, for example `getProduct(4)` in the example would not give 0.
Never resetting at zeros, so the running product of the whole stream grows past 32 bits. The overflow guarantee only covers contiguous products, which the reset prefix always is.
edgeCases: `getProduct(k)` where `k` equals exactly the count of numbers since the last zero: the answer must be `prefix[last] / prefix[0]`, not 0.
`getProduct(k)` immediately after `add(0)`: `prefix = [1]`, so any `k >= 1` must return 0.
A stream with no zeros at all: `k` never exceeds the stream length, so the `[1]` sentinel at the front makes `k = n` return the full product.
Many consecutive zeros, such as `add(0)` repeated: each one resets the array, and queries return 0 until enough non-zero numbers arrive.
Long runs of 1s: prefix values stay constant and the division still works. This is the case that makes the O(k) approaches slow.

takeaways: Range queries over a combine operation that has an inverse (+ with -, × with ÷) can be answered in O(1) using prefix aggregates.
When the inverse fails on a special value (0 for multiplication), ask what that value implies. Here it makes everything before it irrelevant, so you reset rather than patch around it.
A sentinel at the front (`prefix = [1]`) removes the special case for windows that start at the very beginning.
Read overflow guarantees precisely. "Any contiguous product fits" tells you which stored values are safe, and that should shape your design.
